stories.title: Ukraine defends Benghazi strikes as Libya rejects any authorization
stories.summary: On November 24 Kyiv defended its November 22 attacks against Russian vessels in Libyan waters as self-defence. Tripoli rejected allegations of a prior understanding and reiterated that foreign military activity does not excuse violations of Libyan sovereignty.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute extends the implications of the Russia-Ukraine war to a third country and raises questions about international maritime security and the limits of self-defence.
stories.selectionRationale: Fresh competing diplomatic positions on an incident with consequences for Mediterranean security and the scope of an international war.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters, The Kyiv Independent and Anadolu originated separate reports. Ukrainian and Libyan statements are attributed; neither alone decides the legal issue. The Reuters update indicator has no exact revision timestamp. No later developments are used.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: did Kyiv's right to self-defence justify the operation in Libyan waters? Position A: Tykhyi in ly24-a argues Russian military assets are lawful targets under Article 51. Position B: Tripoli in ly24-b says the presence of unauthorized foreign forces does not justify violations of Libyan sovereignty and denies advance agreement. ly24-r corroborates the dispute, not either legal conclusion.

Both sides express concern about Russian military use of third-country infrastructure; they differ on whether Ukrainian action in Libya is justified. The reports do not establish consent or an independent legal ruling.

uncertainties: Whether any relevant authorization or consent existed.
The legal assessment of the operation and any diplomatic response.
The complete consequences for Libyan and regional maritime security.

stories.title: US jury convicts Huawei on ten counts but rejects racketeering conspiracy
stories.summary: A Brooklyn federal jury found Huawei guilty on ten of twelve criminal counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and fraud, while acquitting it of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. The company indicated it would appeal.
stories.whyItMatters: The verdict affects a major telecommunications supplier and a long-running dispute over technology competition, sanctions enforcement and the US-China commercial relationship.
stories.selectionRationale: A major judicial decision involving an internationally important technology supplier, with potential long-term commercial and diplomatic consequences.
stories.evidenceNote: Reuters and AP report the proceedings independently; The Verge's named technology writer synthesizes the DOJ statement and NBC/Bloomberg reporting and sought comment directly. It is not a republished wire story. Al Jazeera's AP/Reuters copy was excluded; NBC page could not be opened and was not selected. The AP date was cross-checked against its same-byline November 24 Washington Post syndication, not counted as an extra source.

commonFacts.text: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei on ten of twelve counts.
The jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Huawei indicated it intended to appeal the convictions.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: does the case establish a company-wide criminal culture, or did prosecutors overgeneralize from individual misconduct? Position A: DOJ official Duva, quoted by hw24-a, describes a systemic pattern spanning years, relying on the prosecuted conduct and guilty verdicts. Position B: Heberlig in hw24-b invokes the acquittals and argues the evidence was selectively assembled from disparate incidents. hw24-r establishes the split verdict; the guilty counts stand, while the jury rejected the racketeering and obstruction conspiracies.
The reports converge on the verdict. The acquittals do not erase the convictions; the convictions do not establish every allegation in the government's broader narrative.

uncertainties: The eventual sentence and financial penalties.
Whether an appeal would change the verdict.
The effects on Huawei's operations and international technology relations.

stories.title: Canada rejects Pentagon criticism of its defence commitment
stories.summary: Canada's defence minister responded on November 24 to a Pentagon fact sheet that questioned Ottawa's military readiness and spending trajectory. David McGuinty maintained that Canada makes its own decisions and that bilateral and NATO cooperation continued.
stories.whyItMatters: The dispute concerns continental defence, NATO commitments and procurement cooperation between closely integrated allies, with consequences for alliance trust.
stories.selectionRationale: A fresh ministerial response to a public disagreement over defence obligations within a major international security alliance.

The Guardian dates release of the memo to Tuesday; TIME and Canadian Press say Monday. commonFacts.text: The Pentagon issued a public fact sheet criticizing Canadian military readiness and spending plans.
Canada and the United States cooperate through NATO and NORAD.
Canada has pledged to reach NATO's new defence and related security spending target by 2035.

framingDifferences.text: Disputed question: is Canada acting as a credible continental defence partner under its current plans? Position A: the Pentagon in ca24-a says readiness and spending are inadequate and cites budget timing and procurement uncertainty. Position B: McGuinty in ca24-b says Canada is sovereign and its operational cooperation continues; Ottawa points to its spending plans and alliance commitments. ca24-r corroborates the criticism and context, not a final readiness assessment.

The accounts agree that spending and procurement are contested. TIME also cites the Canadian budget watchdog's doubts about the long-term spending path. Continued cooperation does not itself prove that every readiness target is met; Pentagon criticism does not establish that cooperation has ceased.

uncertainties: Whether Canada's spending trajectory would meet the 2035 target.
Whether the disagreement would change operational cooperation or alliance trust.

unverifiedClaims.text: The Pentagon characterized Canada as falling short of credible partnership and described longstanding underinvestment.
unverifiedClaims.reason: Attributed official assessment; the selected reporting does not independently audit military readiness.

unverifiedClaims.text: McGuinty maintained that cooperation had not changed.
unverifiedClaims.reason: An official assurance, not a comprehensive independent operational audit.
